props.title: Sisters

sections.content: Brian De Palma's Sisters (1973) marks a pivotal moment in psychological thriller filmmaking, drawing heavily from Hitchcock while establishing De Palma's signature style. The film's split-screen sequences and Bernard Herrmann's haunting score create unbearable tension, particularly during the murder witnessed by Jennifer Salt's character. De Palma's obsession with voyeurism and doubles, which would later define Body Double (1984) and Dressed to Kill (1980), emerges fully formed here. The influence of Psycho (1960) is evident, but De Palma transforms these borrowed elements into something uniquely unsettling.

sections.content: The film's exploration of separated twins draws fascinating parallels with other psychological thrillers like Dead Ringers (1988) and Persona (1966). Margot Kidder's dual performance as Danielle/Dominique establishes a template for identity horror that influenced films like Black Swan (2010). The documentary-style investigation segments, led by Jennifer Salt's determined reporter, anticipate De Palma's later journalistic thriller Blow Out (1981).

De Palma's technical virtuosity in Sisters would influence a generation of thriller directors. The apartment complex setting and themes of urban isolation echo Roman Polanski's Rosemary's Baby (1968), while the clinical horror elements presage David Cronenberg's body horror works like Dead Ringers (1988). The film's exploration of medical experimentation and institutional abuse remains disturbingly relevant. SUBHEAD: Psychological Twin Horror Legacy

sections.content: The success of Sisters helped establish a specific subset of psychological horror focusing on twins and doubles. Films like The Other (1972) and later works such as Goodnight Mommy (2014) build on its foundation of sibling psychological horror. The medical experimentation subplot influenced later institutional horror films like Shutter Island (2010) and A Cure for Wellness (2016).
